title: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
summary: Why memory has a distance on multi-socket servers, how Linux picks a node at first touch, how memory policies and numactl override it, and how to keep threads near their data and verify placement.
outcomes: Explain why NUMA exists and read a node distance table from numactl --hardware
Predict which node a page lands on under first touch and fix a serial initialization bug
Choose between local, bind, preferred and interleave policies with numactl or mbind
Compute average miss latency and bottleneck bandwidth for different page placements
Diagnose placement with numa_maps and numastat, and decide when to use NUMA balancing

lessons.title: Why some memory is farther away than other memory

blocks.md: From the cache hierarchy course you know that a miss in the last-level cache (L3) goes to DRAM and costs far more than a hit. This course asks the next question: on a big server, *which* DRAM? On a machine with several CPU sockets, the answer changes the cost of every cache miss.

The old design is **UMA** (uniform memory access), also called SMP: every CPU reaches all memory through one shared memory controller, so every address costs the same. That shared controller becomes the bottleneck as you add CPUs.

The fix is to give each socket its own memory controller and its own DRAM. Total bandwidth now grows with the number of sockets. The price is **NUMA** (non-uniform memory access): a CPU still sees all memory, but memory attached to its own socket is faster than memory attached to another socket.

Linux calls each group of CPUs plus the memory closest to them a **node**. Memory on the CPU's own node is **local**; memory on any other node is **remote** and is reached over the socket interconnect. The kernel docs stress that these are *cache-coherent* NUMA (ccNUMA) machines: hardware keeps caches coherent across sockets, so programs stay correct no matter where data lives. Only speed changes.

blocks.title: A two-node machine: local and remote paths to DRAM

scenes.caption: Two sockets, each with its own cores, L3 cache, memory controller and DRAM. Linux calls each socket-plus-memory group a node. The sockets are joined by a cache-coherent interconnect.
Local access: a core on node 0 misses in L3 and its own memory controller serves the line from node 0 DRAM. No interconnect hop.
Remote access: the same core reads an address that lives in node 1 DRAM. The request crosses the interconnect and is served by the other socket's controller, which adds latency.
The hotspot: if all data sits on node 0, every core on both sockets queues at memory controller 0 while controller 1 idles, and node 1's traffic also loads the interconnect.

blocks.md: The kernel docs give the reason vendors accept this complexity: NUMA exists to provide scalable memory bandwidth, and that only works if the large majority of cache misses go to local memory. Placement is therefore a software problem, shared by the kernel and your program.

How far is far? Firmware describes it in the ACPI **SLIT** (System Locality Information Table), which Linux exposes as `/sys/devices/system/node/nodeN/distance` and `numactl --hardware` prints as a matrix. A node's distance to itself is defined as 10; other entries are scaled relative to that.

scenes.caption: The distance table Drepper shows for a 4-socket Opteron server, read from /sys/devices/system/node/node*/distance. Row i, column j is the relative cost for node i to reach node j's memory.
ACPI normalizes the diagonal (a node to itself) to 10 and scales the rest relative to it, so 20 means roughly twice the local cost. Values 0 to 9 are reserved and 255 means unreachable.

Drepper points out this table was wrong: each chip has three coherent links and at least one chip must also connect to the Southbridge, so some pair must be two hops apart. Hop counts for a 4-node square (0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3 linked):
So treat the firmware table as a hint. Measure if placement matters: on this AMD design, 2-hop reads cost 30 percent more than local reads but 1-hop reads only 9 percent more.

blocks.title: Access cost by hop count (4-socket Opteron, AMD data)

scenes.caption: Cost relative to a local (0-hop) read, as reported by Drepper from AMD's measurements. Start with reads: local is the 100 percent baseline.
One hop adds 9 percent to a read, two hops add 30 percent. The relative position of core and memory matters, not just local versus remote.
Writes cost more than reads, and distance hurts them too: a 2-hop write is 49 percent slower than a local read and 32 percent slower than a local write (so a local write is about 113 percent).

blocks.md: Drepper also measured this directly: streaming reads from memory one hop away ran about 20 percent slower than from local memory. The exact penalty depends on the machine, but the pattern holds: the more traffic crosses the interconnect, the more you pay in latency, and the more you load a shared link.

Remote memory is not slow like disk. It is the same DRAM, reached through one more hop, typically tens of percent slower per miss. The bigger danger is usually *bandwidth*: when all hot data sits on one node, one memory controller serves every socket while the others idle.
NUMA means the cost of a cache miss depends on which node holds the page. Keep each thread's data on the node where the thread runs.

blocks.question: A program's working set fits entirely in each core's L1 and L2 caches. How much does NUMA placement of its data matter during the steady state?
options: A lot: every load must check the home node of the address first
It matters only for writes, since reads are always served locally
Very little: cache hits never leave the core, so the node only matters on misses
blocks.explain: Placement only changes the cost of requests that go out to DRAM. Hits in private caches are served inside the core no matter which node owns the page. NUMA effects show up when the working set misses the caches, or when cores on different sockets share written cache lines.

blocks.question: A 4-node server's distance table shows 10 on the diagonal and 20 everywhere else. What is the safest reading?
options: Every remote access costs exactly twice a local one
Remote access is roughly twice as costly as local, but firmware tables can be inaccurate, so measure
The machine is actually UMA because all remote entries are equal
blocks.explain: SLIT values are relative estimates normalized to 10 for local access. Drepper shows a real table that reported 20 for every pair even though some pairs had to be two hops apart. Use the table as a hint and benchmark when placement matters.

lessons.title: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node

blocks.md: Recall from the processes course that threads share one address space, and from OS basics (virtual memory) that `malloc` or `mmap` hands out *virtual* addresses. A physical page frame is attached only when the page is first accessed and the kernel handles the page fault. That moment is when Linux picks a node.

The rule comes from the kernel's default policy, **local allocation**: allocate the page on the node of the CPU that triggered the allocation. If that node has no free memory, fall back to other nodes in order of distance. The `set_mempolicy(2)` man page is explicit about timing: for anonymous memory (heap, stack, `MAP_ANONYMOUS`), the policy is applied when the page is *first touched* by a thread. This is widely called the **first-touch** rule.

blocks.prompt: An 8 GiB array is allocated with mmap. The main thread fills it with zeros, then 32 worker threads spread across both nodes each process a slice. Where do the pages live?
blocks.reveal: All of them on the main thread's node. Allocation (mmap) placed nothing; the main thread's writes caused every page fault, and local allocation put each page on the main thread's node. Half the workers now read remote memory for their whole run. The memory was placed by the *initializer*, not the *user*.

blocks.title: Who writes first decides the node

scenes.caption: mmap only reserves 8 GiB of virtual address space. No physical page has been allocated, so no node has been chosen for any of it yet.
Version A: the main thread runs on node 0. Each first write to a page faults, and the default local policy allocates the page on the faulting CPU's node: node 0.
All 2,097,152 pages (8 GiB / 4 KiB) now sit on node 0. Later, workers on node 1 that process the second half will miss to remote memory on every cache miss.
scenes.output: worker on node 1: every DRAM access is remote

scenes.caption: Version B: each worker first pins itself to its node with numa_run_on_node, so the scheduler will keep it on that node's CPUs.
Each worker writes its own half first. Faults now come from both nodes, so pages land where they will later be used.
scenes.output: each worker's DRAM accesses are local

blocks.title: Page placement of an 8 GiB array (one cell = 1 GiB)

scenes.caption: After mmap: nothing is placed (dash). Worker T0 runs on node 0 and will process GiB 0 to 3; worker T1 runs on node 1 and will process GiB 4 to 7.
Serial init (Version A): the main thread on node 0 touches everything first, so every page lands on node 0.
Now the compute phase runs. T0's half is local, but all of T1's 4 GiB are remote: T1 pays the extra hop on every miss, and both workers share controller 0.
Parallel init (Version B): each pinned worker writes its own half first. Placement now matches use, and both memory controllers share the load.

blocks.md:
The fix is to make the initialization look like the computation: same threads, same slices, same CPUs. Two details make it work.

- **Pin the threads.** If the scheduler moves the initializing thread to the other node mid-loop, pages follow the CPU it happened to be on. Pinning with `numa_run_on_node`, `sched_setaffinity` or `numactl --cpunodebind` keeps placement predictable.
- **Use the same partition** in both phases, so each worker touches first exactly the pages it later uses.

Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

Two more consequences of the rule:

- Placement is sticky. A page stays on its node after it is allocated, even if every later user is on another node, unless something migrates it (lesson 5).
- Pages are the unit. A 4 KiB page is placed as a whole, so two threads on different nodes writing adjacent halves of one page share a node for it. With 2 MiB huge pages the unit is 512 times bigger, so per-thread slices need to be larger to land on separate nodes.
malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

blocks.question: A server allocates a large buffer pool at startup and fills it from a single loader thread. Benchmarks show workers on node 1 are slower than workers on node 0. Which change fixes placement with the least code?
options: Call malloc from each worker thread instead of the loader
Add a read-only warm-up pass on each worker after loading
Increase the size of the pool so it spans both nodes
Have each pinned worker write its own share of the pool during startup
blocks.explain: Placement happens on the first write, not on malloc and not on a read (a first read of anonymous memory maps the shared zero page). Having each pinned worker write its share first puts those pages on the worker's node.

blocks.question: Thread A (node 0) and thread B (node 1) each write half of the same 4 KiB page first, at nearly the same moment. Where does the page live?
options: On whichever node's thread faulted first; the other thread's half is remote
Split: 2 KiB on each node
On both nodes, as a coherent copy per node
blocks.explain: A page is the smallest unit of placement. The first fault allocates the whole page on the faulting CPU's node, and the second thread then accesses it remotely. Give each thread page-aligned slices to avoid this.

lessons.title: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave

blocks.md: First touch is just the default. Linux lets you override it with a **memory policy**: a *mode* plus an optional set of nodes. The policy is consulted only when a new page is allocated, so it decides where future pages go, not where existing pages are.

The modes, as described in the kernel's NUMA memory policy guide and `set_mempolicy(2)`:

- **MPOL_LOCAL**: allocate on the faulting CPU's node; fall back to other nodes if it is full. This is what the system default does.
- **MPOL_BIND**: allocate only from the given nodes. If they are full, the allocation fails instead of using another node.
- **MPOL_PREFERRED**: try one node first, then fall back by increasing distance. **MPOL_PREFERRED_MANY** does the same with a set of nodes.
- **MPOL_INTERLEAVE**: spread pages round-robin across the given nodes. **MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE** (Linux 6.9) uses per-node weights from `/sys/kernel/mm/mempolicy/weighted_interleave/`.

blocks.title: Where 8 pages land under each policy (2 nodes)

scenes.caption: A fresh 8-page range, faulted in by a thread running on node 1. Each policy below places the same 8 page faults differently.
Local (default, MPOL_LOCAL): every page goes to the faulting CPU's node, node 1, as long as node 1 has free memory.
Bind to node 0 (MPOL_BIND, numactl --membind=0): pages must come from node 0 even though the thread runs on node 1. If node 0 runs out, the allocation fails rather than spill over.
Preferred node 0 (MPOL_PREFERRED): try node 0 first. Here node 0 fills up after 5 pages, so the kernel falls back to the nearest node with free memory.
Interleave over nodes 0 and 1 (MPOL_INTERLEAVE): node chosen by page offset modulo 2. Which node gets the first page depends on the address; the alternation is what matters.
Weighted interleave with weights 5 and 2 (MPOL_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE): node 0 gets 5 pages for every 2 on node 1. Useful when nodes have unequal bandwidth.

blocks.md: Policies also have a **scope**. From most to least specific: a **VMA policy** on an address range, where a VMA (virtual memory area) is one contiguous mapping such as a heap or an mmap region (set with `mbind`), a **task policy** for a thread and the threads it later creates (set with `set_mempolicy`, inherited across `fork` and `exec`), and the **system default**. Shared memory objects can carry a **shared policy** that every attaching process obeys. A fault uses the most specific policy that exists.

blocks.title: Which policy decides a page fault

scenes.caption: When a page fault needs a new page, the kernel looks for the most specific policy that covers the address. Most programs set none, so the walk ends at the system default.
A process started under numactl --interleave gets a task policy. It covers every allocation of that thread and its children, so the walk stops there.
mbind on an address range installs a VMA policy, the most specific scope for private anonymous memory. It wins over the task policy for that range only.
For System V shared memory or shared anonymous mappings, mbind sets a shared policy on the object itself, so every process that faults pages in obeys it.

blocks.md:
The `numactl` command sets a task policy and then runs your program, so it works on unmodified binaries:

- `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./app` runs on node 0's CPUs and allocates only from node 0.
- `numactl --interleave=all ./bigdatabase` interleaves the whole process across all nodes (an example from the man page).
- `numactl --preferred=1 ./app` prefers node 1 and falls back elsewhere.
- `numactl --hardware` lists nodes, their CPUs, free memory and the distance table.

Inside a program, `mbind` applies a policy to one range, which is how you interleave just a large shared table while keeping per-thread data local. The libnuma library (`numa(3)`) wraps these calls, for example `numa_alloc_onnode` and `numa_alloc_interleaved`.

blocks.caption: Interleave one 1 GiB region across nodes 0 and 1 while the rest of the process keeps the default local policy.

blocks.md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which needs CAP_SYS_NICE). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

Interleave trades latency for bandwidth. With two nodes, half of every thread's misses are remote, but the traffic is spread over both memory controllers. The man page adds a limit: accesses to any *single* page are still served by one node, so a hot small structure gains nothing. Interleave suits large structures shared by all threads with no natural owner, such as a big hash table or a database buffer pool.

Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

blocks.question: A service is started with `numactl --membind=0` on a 2-node box. Node 0 has 64 GiB, node 1 has 64 GiB, and the service grows to 80 GiB. What happens?
options: The extra 16 GiB is allocated on node 1 automatically
The kernel switches the process to interleave mode
Allocations that node 0 cannot satisfy fail, because bind never falls back to node 1
blocks.explain: MPOL_BIND restricts allocation to the listed nodes. numactl(8) says allocation will fail when there is not enough memory on them. If spilling to node 1 is acceptable, use --preferred=0 instead.

blocks.question: You call `mbind(p, len, MPOL_INTERLEAVE, ...)` with flags 0 on a range that the program already filled with data from one thread on node 0. What changes?
options: Existing pages are rebalanced across both nodes immediately
Nothing for existing pages; only pages allocated later in the range are interleaved
The call fails because the range is already populated
blocks.explain: Policies apply at allocation time. Without MPOL_MF_MOVE the existing pages stay on node 0. With MPOL_MF_MOVE the kernel tries to migrate them, though pages already on a listed node are not reshuffled into an interleave.

blocks.question: Which data is the best candidate for interleaving?
options: A 40 GiB hash table read by threads on every node
Each worker thread's private 64 KiB scratch buffer
A 4 KiB counter page updated by all threads
blocks.explain: Interleave helps big structures with no natural owner by spreading their traffic over all controllers. Private buffers belong on their owner's node, and a single page is always on one node, so interleaving a 4 KiB object does nothing.

lessons.title: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth

blocks.md:
Now put numbers on the choices. Two effects matter, and they pull in different directions:

- **Latency**: each remote miss waits longer.
- **Bandwidth**: each memory controller and each interconnect direction can only move so many bytes per second, so where pages live decides which resource saturates first.
Start with latency. If a fraction $f$ of DRAM accesses are remote and remote accesses cost $r$ times the local latency $L$, the average miss latency is a weighted mean.

blocks.caption: Average DRAM latency when a fraction f of misses go to a node r times slower.

blocks.title: Average miss latency vs fraction of remote accesses

x.label: fraction of DRAM misses that are remote

scenes.caption: Model with L = 100 ns and remote 20 percent slower (Drepper's measured one-hop read penalty). Interleaving on 2 nodes makes half the misses remote: 110 ns on average.
A machine with a bigger remote penalty, ratio 2.0 (like a distance of 20 taken literally): interleave now averages 150 ns and all-remote 200 ns.
Simplified: this counts only latency per miss. Real cores overlap many misses, so throughput often depends more on bandwidth, which the next figure models.

blocks.md:
For bandwidth, use a simple bottleneck model. The job finishes when the busiest resource finishes, so time is the maximum of bytes divided by capacity over every controller and link direction.

Assumed machine (round numbers, not a specific product): 2 nodes, 16 threads per node, each memory controller delivers 100 GiB/s, the interconnect carries 40 GiB/s in each direction. The job: 32 threads each stream their own 2 GiB slice, 64 GiB in total, 32 GiB per node's threads.

blocks.tex: T = \max_{\text{resource } k} \frac{\text{bytes through } k}{\text{capacity of } k}
blocks.caption: Bottleneck model: controllers and each link direction are the resources.

blocks.prompt: Under serial init (everything on node 0), which resource limits the run: controller 0 or the interconnect? Compute both times.
blocks.reveal: Controller 0 serves all 64 GiB: 64 / 100 = 0.64 s. Node 1's threads pull their 32 GiB across the link: 32 / 40 = 0.8 s. The **link** is the bottleneck at 0.8 s, an effective 80 GiB/s. The machine has 200 GiB/s of controller bandwidth, and this placement uses 40 percent of it.

blocks.title: Time to stream 64 GiB under four placements (model)

scenes.caption: Serial init: all pages on node 0. Controller 0 must serve 64 GiB (0.64 s), and node 1's 32 GiB must cross the link at 40 GiB/s (0.8 s). The link is the bottleneck: 0.8 s.
Parallel first touch: each node's controller serves its own 32 GiB in 0.32 s, and nothing crosses the link. 0.32 s, an effective 200 GiB/s.
Interleave: controllers each serve 32 GiB (0.32 s), but half of every thread's data is remote, so 16 GiB crosses each link direction (0.4 s). 0.4 s: good, with no code change.
Run only on node 0 (cpunodebind=0, membind=0): all accesses local, but one controller serves 64 GiB (0.64 s) and half the cores sit idle. Local is not enough; you also need both controllers.

blocks.md:
The four results, effective bandwidth = 64 GiB / time:

1. Serial init: 0.8 s, 80 GiB/s.
2. Parallel first touch: 0.32 s, 200 GiB/s.
3. Interleave: 0.4 s, 160 GiB/s.
4. Node 0 only: 0.64 s, 100 GiB/s.

The fix from lesson 2 is worth 2.5x here, and it costs a few lines of code. Interleave recovers most of it without touching code, which is why `numactl --interleave=all` is a common first step for software that cannot be changed.

Simplified model: it ignores caches, assumes perfect overlap, symmetric links and that threads can saturate their controller. Real numbers differ by machine, so measure with your workload. The *ordering* of the options is what the model teaches.

Good NUMA placement does two things at once: it keeps misses local (latency) and it spreads traffic over every memory controller (bandwidth). Losing either one can cost more than the latency penalty alone suggests.

blocks.question: In the model, the interconnect is upgraded to 80 GiB/s per direction. What is the new time for the interleave placement?
blocks.explain: Each link direction now carries 16 GiB at 80 GiB/s = 0.2 s, but each controller still needs 32 / 100 = 0.32 s. The maximum is 0.32 s, so interleave now matches parallel first touch in bandwidth (its misses are still slower on average).

blocks.question: A latency-bound service (pointer chasing, one outstanding miss at a time) runs one thread per node. Which placement is best for it?
options: Keep each thread's data on its own node
Interleave all memory, to use both controllers
Bind everything to node 0 for predictability
blocks.explain: With one outstanding miss at a time, bandwidth is not the limit; every miss pays the latency. Local placement gives f = 0, the lowest average latency. Interleave would make half the misses remote.

lessons.title: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis

blocks.md: Placement is half the problem. The other half is that threads move. The kernel's NUMA overview explains that the scheduler knows the topology (through scheduling domains) and tries not to migrate tasks to distant nodes, but under enough load imbalance a task can still move to another node, away from the memory it already allocated.

There are two ways to keep threads and data together.

- **Pin**: restrict the thread to one node's CPUs with `taskset`, `numactl --cpunodebind`, `sched_setaffinity(2)` or `numa_run_on_node`. Placement becomes predictable. The cost is flexibility: the scheduler can no longer move work to idle CPUs elsewhere.
- **Let the kernel move memory**: **automatic NUMA balancing** (sysctl `kernel.numa_balancing`) watches which node accesses each page and migrates pages toward their users.

Automatic NUMA balancing, per the kernel sysctl docs, works by sampling: it periodically unmaps pages of a task and traps the resulting page faults (NUMA *hinting* faults). At fault time it knows which CPU touched which page, and decides whether the page should be migrated to the local node. Scan rate is tunable through `scan_delay_ms`, `scan_period_min_ms`, `scan_period_max_ms` and `scan_size_mb` under `/sys/kernel/debug/sched/numa_balancing/`.

blocks.title: Automatic NUMA balancing with hinting faults

scenes.caption: The thread runs on node 1, but its page P sits on node 0 (placed by an earlier first touch). Every miss on P is remote.
Periodically the kernel scans the next chunk (scan size) of the task's address space and unmaps those pages so the next access traps.
The thread touches P again and takes a NUMA hinting fault. This fault exists only to sample who accesses what.
The handler sees the access came from node 1 while P lives on node 0, and decides P should move. Simplified: real kernels apply heuristics before migrating.
The mapping is restored and the access completes. Later misses on P are local. The cost was a fault plus a page copy.
If pages are found well placed, the scan delay grows and sampling slows; if not, it shrinks. Overhead tracks how wrong placement is.

blocks.md: Balancing is not free. The kernel docs say the unmapping and extra faults cost overhead that is *ideally* offset by better locality, with no universal guarantee, and that it should be disabled when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes. Workloads that are already pinned and carefully placed are the natural candidates to turn it off.

To diagnose placement, read what the kernel already counts.

- `numactl --hardware`: nodes, CPUs per node, free memory per node, distances.
- `/proc/PID/numa_maps`: one line per memory range with its policy and `N0=`, `N1=` page counts per node. This is the ground truth for *where a process's pages are*.
- `numastat` or `/sys/devices/system/node/node*/numastat`: per-node allocation counters.

The numastat counters, from the kernel docs:

- `numa_hit`: a process wanted this node and got it.
- `numa_miss`: a process wanted another node but got memory from this node.
- `numa_foreign`: a process wanted this node but got memory from another node.
- `local_node` / `other_node`: the allocating process ran on this node / on another node.
- `interleave_hit`: interleaving wanted this node and succeeded.

All of them count **allocations**, not memory accesses.

blocks.prompt: Recall the serial-init example: the main thread on node 0 allocates 64 GiB (16,777,216 pages of 4 KiB), then threads on both nodes read it. What do node 0's numastat counters show for those pages?
blocks.reveal: 16,777,216 more `numa_hit` and `local_node`, and zero `numa_miss`. Every allocation was local *to the allocating thread*, so the counters look perfect. Yet half the later reads are remote. numastat cannot see this; `numa_maps` (all pages on N0) plus knowing where the workers run can, and so can hardware performance counters for remote DRAM accesses.

blocks.md: Writes shared across nodes are costly even with perfect page placement: each write moves the cache line between sockets through the coherence protocol. The kernel's own memory policy code avoids atomic reference counting on hot paths for exactly this reason (cache lines bouncing between CPUs and NUMA nodes). Keep frequently written data, like counters and locks, per node.

A practical checklist for a NUMA server:

1. Check the topology with `numactl --hardware`.
2. Decide ownership: private data stays with its thread; big shared data is interleaved.
3. Initialize in parallel from the threads that will use the data, and pin those threads.
4. Verify with `numa_maps` and measure. Turn automatic balancing off only if the workload is bound and placement is already right.
Locality needs both halves: pages on the right node, and threads that stay there. Pin, or let NUMA balancing migrate pages, and verify placement with numa_maps rather than allocation counters.

blocks.question: A database pins each worker to one node and places every buffer with explicit mbind policies. Profiling shows time spent in page faults on pages that never move. What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable MPOL_INTERLEAVE on all buffers
Use smaller pages so faults are cheaper
Disable automatic NUMA balancing for this workload
blocks.explain: These are NUMA hinting faults from automatic balancing sampling pages that are already correctly placed. The kernel docs recommend disabling balancing when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes.

blocks.question: numastat shows numa_miss = 0 and numa_foreign = 0 on every node, yet threads on node 1 see slow memory. Which explanation fits?
options: Allocations were local to the allocating thread, but the pages are used by threads on another node
The counters are broken on this kernel
Node 1 has no memory, so its CPUs never miss
blocks.explain: numastat counts where allocations were satisfied relative to the allocator's preference. A single initializer thread produces perfect counters while the consumers on node 1 read remotely. Check /proc/PID/numa_maps for page locations.

blocks.question: An API server's threads are spread over both nodes and the scheduler often moves them. Each request touches small, short-lived data. What is a reasonable default?
options: Pin every thread and bind all memory to node 0
Leave the default local policy, and consider automatic NUMA balancing rather than hand placement
Interleave all memory with numactl --interleave=all
blocks.explain: Short-lived per-request data is usually allocated and used by the same thread, so local allocation already places it well. Hard pinning removes scheduler flexibility, and binding to one node wastes the other controller. Hand tuning pays off for large, long-lived data.
